extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, damages experts, IP economists, licensing professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and evaluating reasonable-royalty damages analyses in patent litigation, especially the use and limits of the Georgia‑Pacific factors and preferred economic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (the 15 factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conspectus of fifteen evidentiary factors originally listed in Georgia‑Pacific v. U.S. Plywood that courts and experts commonly consider in reasonable royalty analyses (covering past technology agreements; nature, scope, and duration of the license; licensing policy; commercial relationship; sales of non‑patented items; sales and profits; contribution of the patented technology; expert opinions; and the hypothetical negotiation outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts the typical practice of marching through all fifteen factors and notes what the factors roughly cover. It also emphasizes that the Georgia‑Pacific list is a historically important checklist but not a formula—experts often mark each factor as having an “upward,” “downward,” or “neutral” effect, though that practice has limitations. Use the list as a menu of possible considerations, not as a mechanical calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat Georgia‑Pacific factors as mutually exclusive or collectively exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the Georgia‑Pacific factors are neither mutually exclusive nor collectively exhaustive with respect to relevant economic issues in a reasonable royalty analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factors overlap (e.g., factor 12 and 13 overlap economically) and other relevant economic considerations may exist beyond the fifteen. Experts should avoid double-counting the same economic consideration under multiple factors and should consider additional case‑specific factors where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze only factors relevant to the specific record
rubrics_metrics.description: Include and emphasize only those Georgia‑Pacific factors (or other considerations) that are actually relevant to the factual record of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Ericsson v. D‑Link, courts and experts should avoid instructing juries or testifying about multiple Georgia‑Pacific factors that are not relevant or are misleading on the record. Listing irrelevant factors can confuse the trier of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide depth of analysis and explain extent of impact
rubrics_metrics.description: When using factors, experts must explain why and generally to what extent a particular factor impacts the royalty calculation rather than making conclusory remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WhitServe calls for concentrating on fully analyzing applicable factors, not cursorily reciting all fifteen. Mathematical precision is not required, but some explanation of both why and to what extent the factor affects the royalty is needed. Anti‑pattern: reciting a factor and making a conclusory 'up/down/neutral' remark without supporting explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on fundamentally flawed starting points or rules of thumb
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using discredited or arbitrary starting points (e.g., the 25% rule) as the basis for a royalty analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniloc v. Microsoft holds that beginning from a fundamentally flawed premise and then adjusting it still results in a flawed conclusion. If a starting point is used, it must be economically defensible and supported by the record; otherwise the entire analysis may be unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vacuous directional adjustments without a defensible baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Directional 'upward'/'downward'/'neutral' assignments to factors are unhelpful unless tied to a defensible starting point and explained quantitatively or qualitatively in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts sometimes apply directional adjustments without specifying a starting point or without linking adjustments to facts. Such vacuous adjustments provide limited insight and can be misleading. Always state the baseline, why adjustments are needed, and how large they are (or their qualitative justification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on sound economic principles applied to case‑specific facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer an economic, fact‑centric approach that applies sound economic principles to the particular facts of the case rather than rote iteration of all Georgia‑Pacific factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends using economic valuation approaches (e.g., comparing two otherwise identical products that differ only by the patented feature) and organizing analysis around the most relevant economic information. This approach will often, but not necessarily explicitly, address many Georgia‑Pacific considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty must reflect value attributable to the infringing features (and no more)
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of royalty base and rate must reflect the value attributable to the infringing features of the product and must not compensate for unrelated value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Garretson and Dowagiac, the article highlights the governing legal principle that reasonable royalties should compensate for the value of what was taken—the patented technology—and should not exceed that value. This is a core conceptual check on any royalty estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple reasonable methods are acceptable; choose method(s) suited to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts recognize multiple acceptable approaches to calculating reasonable royalties (e.g., established royalties, infringer's profit projections, or hypothetical negotiation analyses) and one or more may be appropriate depending on the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Wordtech and Apple v. Motorola, different methods have strengths and weaknesses; experts should select methods that fit the available evidence and explain why the chosen method(s) are appropriate for the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court/ fact‑finder must determine a reasonable royalty from the record even if evidence is incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when the record does not fully support either party’s royalty estimate, the fact‑finder must still determine what royalty is supported by the record as a minimum floor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple v. Motorola emphasizes the duty to arrive at some reasonable royalty based on the record. This means experts should make the best-supported inferences while disclosing limitations and uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no formulaic weighting or precise ordering of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no prescribed formula, precise ranking, or automatic transduction of the Georgia‑Pacific factors into pecuniary equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Georgia‑Pacific court itself warned that 'there is no formula by which these factors can be rated precisely in the order of their relative importance.' Experts should avoid presenting the factors as a mechanical scoring system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of double‑counting due to factor overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many Georgia‑Pacific factors interpenetrate, experts must structure analysis to avoid redundantly crediting the same economic consideration under multiple factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides the example of factor 12 (customary portion of profit/selling price) overlapping with factor 13 (portion of realizable profit credited to the invention). Recognize overlaps and consolidate or explain how separate factors produce distinct effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize expert testimony around the most economically informative order
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the analysis in an order that is logically and economically informative for the facts at hand rather than mechanically following the fifteen‑factor list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lucent and Ericsson are cited to support flexible analysis; a focused, fact‑driven presentation is more helpful to the trier of fact than a rote sequential recital of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use market‑based comparables and incremental‑value approaches where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When available, use market comparisons (e.g., price/profit differences between otherwise identical products differing only by the asserted feature) to quantify the value of the patented technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article analogizes to real estate comparables (e.g., two similar houses, one with a pool) as a valid economic approach that inherently reflects many Georgia‑Pacific considerations without explicit recitation.
